name: Whey Protein
lead: Whey protein is a mixture of proteins isolated from whey, the liquid by-product of cheese making. Its main components are beta-lactoglobulin, alpha-lactalbumin, serum albumin and immunoglobulins, and it is sold mainly as a powdered protein supplement in concentrate, isolate and hydrolysate forms.[1][25] It is usually stirred into water or milk as a shake, or blended into smoothies, oats and baked goods.

For appearance, whey is used as a convenient way to reach daily protein targets while lifting: protein supplies the amino acids that muscle is built and repaired from, so shakes are used to support muscle size and shape during bulks and to help hold on to lean mass during diets, the combination many lifters call a leaner, fuller physique. Whey is digested quickly and is rich in leucine, an amino acid that signals muscle protein synthesis.[20][21][22]

A 2018 meta-analysis of 49 trials with 1,863 participants found that protein supplementation during prolonged resistance training modestly increased strength, fat-free mass and muscle size, with smaller effects on fat-free mass in older participants.[2] A 2024 network meta-analysis of 116 trials examined how timing and protein type affect results.[3] In 2010 a European Food Safety Authority panel concluded there was no evidence supporting weight-loss claims for whey and that it is roughly as effective as other protein sources for building strength and lean mass.[1]

Reviews of adverse effects associate chronic, excessive use with possible kidney, liver, acne and microbiota concerns, while other researchers have argued that some of these claims are unsubstantiated.[4][5] Whey acne is one of the most discussed appearance questions about it, and a 2024 randomised trial in young men with acne examined it directly.[17]
infobox: By-product of cheese production; about 20% of cow's milk protein [1]
Isolates are typically over 90% protein by dry weight [1]
Soluble whey protein for beverages from 1969-1971 [1]
Fast: sharp, short rise in blood amino acids [20]
Lactose (concentrates), milk allergy, acne discussion, heavy metals in some products [1][4][23]

paras: Whey is the liquid left when milk is coagulated with acid or rennet. Protein is concentrated mainly by membrane filtration (microfiltration then ultrafiltration, followed by spray-drying) or ion-exchange chromatography.[1] Cow's milk protein is roughly 20 percent whey and 80 percent casein, and the main whey fractions are named in dairy-science nomenclature.[1][25]

Whey protein concentrates retain some lactose and fat; isolates are processed to exceed 90 percent protein by dry weight; hydrolysates are partially pre-digested and costlier; native whey is taken from skim milk and lacks glycomacropeptide.[1] Wikipedia says whey appears more bioavailable than casein or soy protein.[1] Protein supplements more broadly come as powders, bars and ready-to-drink shakes, from whey, plant or meat sources, with premium powders reaching around 30 g of protein per scoop.[23]

Whey produces a large but short rise in blood amino acids after a meal. In a 1997 study using isotope-labelled milk proteins, whey stimulated whole-body protein synthesis by 68 percent, versus 31 percent for casein, while casein, which empties from the stomach slowly, gave a prolonged plateau and inhibited protein breakdown.[20]

In a 2009 study of 18 young men who trained one leg, drinks matched for essential amino acids gave about 122 percent greater post-exercise muscle protein synthesis with whey hydrolysate than with casein and 31 percent greater than with soy.[21] A dose-response study with egg protein found muscle protein synthesis after leg exercise was maximal at about 20 g of protein.[24] The International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand describes whey as stimulating muscle protein synthesis more than soy or casein in acute studies and suggests per-meal protein of roughly 0.25 g per kg, or 20 to 40 g.[22]

Lifters use whey shakes to reach daily protein targets, as a meal supplement or snack during cutting diets, and after training. T Nation logs show protein shakes added to meal plans and used in place of meals in diet phases.[6][7] The ISSN position stand puts protein for most exercising people at about 1.4 to 2.0 g per kg of body weight per day, with higher intakes of 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg suggested for resistance-trained people trying to retain lean mass while restricting calories.[22]

Wikipedia's article on protein supplements notes that a meta-analysis found no extra gains above roughly 1.6 g per kg per day in younger people, while it suggests about 2.2 g per kg for those maximising training gains.[23] That article also states that pre- and post-workout timing has not been shown to matter and that total daily intake is what counts, whereas the ISSN stand says both pre- and post-workout intake can be beneficial and spaces doses about every 3 to 4 hours.[23][22]

Whey is studied for sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss), often combined with leucine, vitamin D or exercise, and in clinical nutrition.[8][9][10][11] Hydrolysed whey is used in hypoallergenic infant formulas, though whey proteins are responsible for some milk allergies, with caseins the major allergens.[1]

The 2018 meta-analysis reported mean increases with protein supplementation of 2.49 kg in one-repetition-maximum strength and 0.30 kg in fat-free mass, plus gains in muscle fibre and mid-femur cross-sectional area, with effects diminishing with age and with higher baseline protein intake.[2] The 2024 network meta-analysis found that post-exercise and night-time protein supplementation improved fat-free mass, skeletal muscle mass or handgrip strength versus placebo.[3] Other meta-analyses examined recovery of muscle function, strength and body mass, and differences among concentrated, hydrolysed and isolated whey on body composition.[12][13][14]

In older adults, a one-year randomized trial examined daily protein supplementation with or without resistance training on muscle size, strength and function; the PROVIDE trial and other trials tested vitamin D and leucine-enriched whey in sarcopenia, and meta-analyses address whey with or without vitamin D or resistance training.[8][9][10][11][15]

A 2020 randomized trial compared whey and pea protein for post-eccentric exercise muscle damage.[16] An allergy task-force review examined dietary interventions for atopic dermatitis skin symptoms in children.[18]

Researchers describe acne exacerbation after whey as inconclusive among experts. A 2024 double-blind, randomised noninferiority trial in Thailand enrolled 49 men with mild to moderate acne (mean age about 20) and gave one group 30 g of whey protein daily with a non-whey supplement and the other group a non-whey supplement for six months. Total acne lesion counts on the face and trunk did not differ significantly between groups, and the authors concluded whey was noninferior for total lesion change and severity.[17] A systematic review of diet and acne examines how glycaemic load and dairy relate to insulin, IGF-1 and androgens.[26]

A 2021 systematic review of 11 documents concluded that most papers linked damaging effects to chronic and excessive whey use, mainly in kidneys and liver, with other studies reporting associations with aggression, acne and microbiota changes, aggravated by sedentary lifestyle.[4] A published discussion of that review argued that claims of adverse effects of whey on kidney and liver function were unsubstantiated.[5] Wikipedia's protein supplement article notes that people with severe kidney disease who are not on dialysis may need to limit protein.[23]

Whey contains lactose in concentrates and is a milk allergen for some people.[1] Wikipedia also reports that Consumer Reports found about two-thirds of tested protein products had lead above a safe threshold per serving, with plant-based products higher than dairy or whey products though whey products were still elevated, and some products had cadmium and arsenic levels of concern.[23]

By the late 1960s surplus whey was an economic and environmental problem for the New Zealand dairy industry. In 1969 Coca-Cola Export Corporation executive Alex Malaspina asked the New Zealand Dairy Board for soluble whey protein for acidic carbonated drinks, which led to development of beverage-grade concentrate (a 65 percent protein concentrate was produced by ultrafiltration in 1970) and to Tai, a whey-fortified drink launched by Coca-Cola in Brazil in 1971.[1] By the late 1980s whey proteins were gaining importance in sports nutrition, weight management and medical nutrition, and the dairy industry later consolidated into Fonterra in 2001.[1]

In the research literature, the 1997 isotope study of fast versus slow milk proteins and McMaster University's studies in 2009 comparing whey, casein and soy are among the often-cited works behind the 'fast protein' idea.[20][21] The 2018 BJSM meta-analysis and the 2017 ISSN position stand are common references for intake and supplementation questions.[2][22]

In lifting forums whey is a default supplement, mentioned in meal logs and as a convenient protein source, and appears in jokes about protein shakes.[6][7][19] Appearance-focused communities weigh it against concerns about skin, and users sometimes switch to isolate or plant proteins when they associate shakes with breakouts.
Related practices discussed alongside whey include creatine, casein before sleep, mass-gainer powders, meal-replacement shakes and plant proteins such as pea and rice.[22]

lore.intro: Whey is treated in physique communities as an ordinary protein source, with occasional debate over acne and kidney effects.[6][7]

claims.believers: Lifters add shakes to meal plans to hit protein goals during training.[6][7]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report modest gains in strength and lean mass with protein supplementation, smaller in older and higher-intake groups; EFSA judged whey about as effective as other proteins.[1][2]

claims.claim: Whey is the best protein for muscle because it is digested fast and is high in leucine
claims.believers: Posts treat whey as the gold-standard shake for building size.
claims.experts: Acute studies found greater muscle protein synthesis after whey than casein or soy, and the ISSN stand says whey stimulates synthesis more than soy or casein acutely; the Wikipedia protein supplement article says total daily intake matters most and EFSA judged whey about as effective as other proteins for strength and lean mass.[21][22][23][1]

claims.claim: You must drink a shake within about 30 minutes of training
claims.believers: Gym lore often treats a post-workout shake as time-critical.
claims.experts: The ISSN stand says pre- and post-workout intakes both give benefit and best timing may be individual; Wikipedia states there is no evidence that timing matters when total intake is equal; a 2024 network meta-analysis reported benefit with post-exercise and night-time dosing.[22][23][3]

claims.believers: Shakes are used as meal replacements in cutting phases.[7]
claims.experts: The 2010 EFSA panel found no evidence supporting weight-loss claims; the ISSN position stand suggests higher protein intakes may help retain lean mass during calorie restriction.[1][22]

claims.believers: Users commonly report skin breakouts after starting shakes, and some stop or switch products.
claims.experts: A systematic review lists acne among reported associations, while a 2024 six-month double-blind trial in 49 men found whey noninferior to a non-whey supplement for total acne lesions.[4][17]

claims.believers: Concern circulates around heavy protein use.
claims.experts: A 2021 review linked chronic abusive use to organ effects while a published discussion called such claims unsubstantiated; Wikipedia notes people with severe kidney disease may need to limit protein.[4][5][23]

claims.claim: Plant proteins give the same results as whey
claims.believers: Vegan lifters and those avoiding dairy report similar progress with pea or rice powders.
claims.experts: A randomised trial compared whey and pea protein after eccentric exercise, and ISSN notes rice protein gave similar body-composition changes to whey in one 8-week study.[16][22]

claims.claim: Protein powders can carry heavy metals
claims.believers: Online discussion of product testing makes brand and third-party testing a theme in supplement threads.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports Consumer Reports found about two-thirds of tested protein products had lead above a safe threshold per serving, with plant-based higher than whey products.[23]

chain: Whey adds fast-digesting, leucine-rich protein to the day
Higher protein intake supports muscle repair and growth after resistance training

angle.text: Lifters use whey shakes to reach their daily protein target alongside training, so that muscle can be built or kept while eating for size or for leanness. The shake itself is a convenient protein source; the physique change comes through training and total diet.
